newsitem.title: UK: Irish guerrillas blamed for killing Protestant.
newsitem.headline: Irish guerrillas blamed for killing Protestant.

text.p: A Protestant politician accused Irish republicans of trying to foment fresh Northern Ireland strife on Wednesday after a gunman killed a leading former guerrilla in a Belfast Protestant stronghold.
The killing happened two hours before Britain's Queen Elizabeth arrived in the province for the first time since the collapse of an Irish Republican Army ceasefire in February last year.

"I think there's no doubt that republicans were responsible for this assassination," Ulster Democratic Party leader Gary McMichael said as anger swept the staunchly pro-British Loyalist area where Robert "Basher" Bates was shot earlier.

"It would appear that their intention is to try and bring all of our society back into a full-scale conflict situation," McMichael, whose party is the political arm of banned UDA Loyalist guerrillas, told Sky Television.
"I think that the situation is grave indeed," said McMichael who has played a vital role in persuading underground Loyalist commanders not to abandon a fragile ceasefire.

No group admitted responsibility for the murder of Bates, one of the so-called "Shankill Butchers" gang that carried out a wave of gruesome knife murders of 19 Catholic nationalists in the early 1970s.

Urging Protestant extremists not to strike back, senior Loyalist politician Billy Hutchinson, of the Progressive Unionist Party, said Bates believed that the way forward for the troubled province was through political dialogue.
"I would appeal to Loyalists not to retaliate. This man would not have wanted that...I have to say that I would be concerned about the next 48 hours," Hutchinson told reporters.

Loyalist sources suspected either the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which has killed two soldiers in the past year, or a left-wing splinter group, the Irish National Liberation Army, which killed an off-duty policeman in a bar, last month.

Loyalists support continued British rule in Northern Ireland, where Protestants outnumber Roman Catholics three to two. The IRA is fighting to end British rule and unite the province with the overwhelmingly Catholic Irish Republic.
Security was tight for Queen Elizabeth's one-day visit, during which she was due to meet schoolchildren and charity workers.
Marksmen, on alert for republican guerrillas, were on rooftops in a rural town that she visited, and security vehicles were positioned on motorway roadbridges.
Bates was released earlier this year after serving 19 years in prison. Friends said he was a totally reformed character and had zealously embraced religion as a born-again Christian.
He was working in an office with a group that rehabilitates former prisoners when at least one gunman calmly walked in and shot him at close range before running off.
John White, a close political associate of McMichael, said the killing could have "profound consequences" for Loyalists already shaky ceasefire.
"Obviously this man was well respected in this community...It is a new twist in the IRA's campaign," he told Reuters.

Loyalists said it was the first time a former prisoner had been specifically attacked by either side since a faltering peace process started in September 1994 after the IRA called a truce and Loyalists followed suit six weeks later.
Multi-party talks have been under way for the past year but have failed to ease divisions.
